title: Peaks and Dips Along a Trail
statement:
A trail is sampled as an array heights. A run of neighbouring equal heights is a flat stretch and counts as one spot.

A spot is a peak if the nearest different height on its left and the nearest different height on its right are both lower. It is a dip if both are higher. A spot that has no different height on one of its sides (for example the start or end of the trail) is neither.

Return the total number of peaks plus dips.

examples.why: The flat 5, 5 is one peak (3 on the left, 2 on the right). The 2 is a dip (5 and 4). The flat 4, 4, 4 sits between 2 and 7, so it is neither.
The flat 6s have nothing different on their left, and 1 has nothing on its right.
Peak, dip, peak. The two ends never count.

hints: Flat stretches are the only thing that makes this tricky. What if they were squashed into a single element?
Remove consecutive duplicates first. Now every spot has a different height directly on each side.
In the squashed array, count the interior positions that are higher than both neighbours or lower than both. You can do it in one pass by remembering the last different height.

explain.intuition:
Flat stretches are the whole difficulty. If you squash every run of equal heights into one element, each spot's nearest different neighbours become its direct neighbours, and a peak or dip is just an element higher or lower than both sides.

You do not even need the squashed copy. Walk the array keeping prev, the last height that differed from the current run. Skip an element while it equals the next one, so each run is judged once, at its last element. There, compare prev, the current height and the next height, which is guaranteed to differ.
steps: Build flat: copy heights, skipping any value equal to the one just copied.
For each interior index i of flat (1 to length − 2):
If flat[i] is greater than both neighbours, or smaller than both, add one.
pitfalls: Comparing only with the direct neighbours of the original array. In [3, 5, 5, 2] neither 5 is higher than both of its direct neighbours, yet the stretch is a peak.
Counting every element of a flat peak separately: [2, 7, 7, 7, 7, 2] has one peak, not four.
Counting the first or last stretch. It has no different height on one side, so it is never a peak or dip.

complexity.space: O(n) for the squashed copy, O(1) for the one-pass version

solutions.title: Look outward from every run
solutions.idea: For the first index of each run, scan left and right for the nearest different heights and compare.

solutions.title: Squash runs, then compare neighbours
solutions.idea: After removing consecutive duplicates, a peak or dip is an interior element above or below both neighbours.

solutions.title: One pass with the last different height
solutions.idea: Skip an element when it equals the next one. Otherwise compare it with the last different height on the left and the next element.

followups: Report the index range of every peak stretch instead of a count.
Heights stream in one at a time. Keep the count up to date with O(1) memory.
lcTitle: Count Hills and Valleys in an Array
